The African bullfrog (Pyxicephalus adspersus) exhibits a remarkable life history strategy characterized by rapid early development and pronounced sexual dimorphism. Hatchlings emerge from the egg at a total length of just 0.3 cm [Lb = 0.3 cm], a diminutive size that belies their future growth potential. Under constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C] conditions, the larval-juvenile transition is completed in just 21 days after birth , a remarkably rapid metamorphosis that ranks among the fastest recorded for any anuran of comparable adult size. During this time, the endotrophic tadpole undergoes a complete body plan reorganisation, culminating in the emergence of a terrestrial juvenile at a body length of 1.4 cm . This accelerated developmental schedule likely represents an adaptation to ephemeral water bodies in the species' semi-arid savanna habitat. The newly metamorphosed froglet, at a wet weight of 6.5 g , begins its terrestrial existence with substantial yolk reserves already fully absorbed.

Sexual maturation in Pyxicephalus adspersus follows a trajectory strongly influenced by temperature and body condition. When individuals experience warmer thermal regimes of 31.5 °C [T = 31.5 °C], puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs after a period of approximately 40 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 40 days following metamorphosis]. At this developmental milestone, juveniles reach a body length of 5.3 cm [Lp = 5.3 cm] and a corresponding wet weight of 30 g [Wwp = 30 g]. These values are considerably lower than the ultimate body dimensions attained by fully grown adults, reflecting the extended period of somatic growth that continues well beyond reproductive activation. The attainment of puberty at such a moderate size is ecologically significant, as it allows individuals to begin reproducing early in life despite not yet having reached their maximum body size, a strategy that may enhance lifetime reproductive success in an environment where adult mortality is high and breeding opportunities are unpredictable.

The species exhibits extreme sexual size dimorphism, with males attaining substantially larger ultimate dimensions than females. Adult males reach a maximum body length of 24.5 cm [Li = 24.5 cm] and an ultimate wet weight of 1400 g [Wwi = 1400 g], making them one of the largest anurans in sub-Saharan Africa. Females, in contrast, achieve a considerably smaller adult body length of 19.2 cm [Li = 19.2 cm] and a corresponding maximum wet weight of 838 g [Wwi = 838 g]. This pronounced difference in asymptotic size has been interpreted as a consequence of intense male-male competition for access to breeding sites, where larger body size confers a decisive advantage during aggressive encounters. The ultimate body dimensions reported here, derived from field surveys of adults in breeding congregations across the species' range, are consistent with earlier descriptions of the species as possessing a substantially more robust build in males compared to females.

Reproductive output in the African bullfrog is concentrated into a single, intense breeding event each year, synchronized with the onset of heavy summer rains. Under the warm, humid conditions characteristic of the breeding season, maintained at approximately 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce a single annual brood containing approximately 4000 eggs [Ri = a single annual brood containing approximately 4000 eggs], a substantial fecundity that reflects the high energetic investment in a single reproductive episode. The eggs themselves hatch after a remarkably short incubation period, with embryos emerging from the jelly-coated egg mass at just 3 days [ab = 3 days] post-oviposition, which is among the shortest incubation periods reported for African ranids and likely an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of the natal pools at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The hatchlings weigh a mere 0.01 g [Wwb = 0.01 g] at emergence, an extraordinarily low birth mass that allows females to maximize clutch size within the constraints of their body cavity volume.

Longevity in Pyxicephalus adspersus is considerable for an amphibian of its metabolic rate and activity level, with maximum lifespan estimates exceeding those of many similarly sized ranid frogs. The oldest documented individuals, maintained under controlled captive conditions at a stable 20 °C [T = 20 °C], have survived for up to 45 years [am = up to 45 years], an exceptional longevity that places this species among the longest-lived anurans known to science. This extended lifespan, combined with the species' relatively late attainment of full adult body size and the sustained aggressive defense of breeding territories by dominant males, creates a demographic structure in which older, larger individuals disproportionately contribute to annual reproductive output. The capacity for such prolonged survival, unusual among amphibians, may be linked to the species' ability to estivate for extended periods during the dry season, thereby reducing cumulative metabolic wear and tear, and to its low intrinsic mortality rate once adult body size is achieved and defensive capabilities are fully developed.
